docs.title: DataGEMS Data Workflow Orchestrator
docs.text:
This is the documentation site for the DataGEMS Data Workflow Orchestrator. The service is part of the wider DataGEMS platform. This is part of the overall platform documentation.

The platform Data Workflow Orchestrator service acts as the horizontal data processing workflow solution for DataGEMS serving dataset onboarding, profiling and indexing tasks.

You can use the menu options on the left to navigate through the available documentation. You may be interested to jump directly to an Architecture Overview, see the available Onboarding Material or see some Workflow Examples. You can find here the service code repository.

For any questions, you can consult the FAQ, check if there is a relevant issue answering your question or contact the DataGEMS Help Desk.

docs.title: Service Architecture
docs.text: This service is built using the Apache/Airflow tool. Apache Airflow is an open-source platform for developing, scheduling, and monitoring batch-oriented workflows. It offers an extensible Python framework that enables us to build workflows connecting with virtually any technology. A web-based UI helps us visualize, manage, and debug our workflows. For how the orchestrator fits into the wider DataGEMS platform, see Platform Integration; for the workflows it offers, see the Workflow Overview.

docs.title: Why Apache Airflow
docs.text: Apache Airflow was selected as the orchestration layer for this solution because it provides explicit, observable, and resilient workflow coordination across multiple services. The platform is particularly well-suited for environments where execution order, timing, and reliability are first-class architectural concerns. Rather than embedding orchestration logic inside individual services, Airflow centralizes workflow control while keeping services loosely coupled and independently deployable.

docs.title: Explicit Workflow Orchestration
docs.text:
In Airflow, workflows are defined declaratively using "Directed Acyclic Graphs", in short DAGs. Inside a DAG, dependencies between execution steps are explicit, deterministic and inspectable. These individual execution pieces of work are called Tasks, arranged with dependencies and data flows taken into account.

A Dag specifies the dependencies between tasks, which defines the order in which to execute the tasks. Tasks describe what to do, be it fetching data, running analysis, triggering other systems, or more.

docs.title: Workflows as code
docs.text:
Airflow workflows are defined entirely in Python. This "workflows as code" approach brings several advantages:

  • Dynamic: Pipelines are defined in code, enabling dynamic DAG generation and parameterization.
  • Extensible: The Airflow framework includes a wide range of built-in operators and can be further extended to cover a wide variety of programming needs.

docs.title: Centralized Control Without Centralized Logic
docs.text:
Airflow acts as a control plane, not a business logic engine:

  • Services remain autonomous and focused on domain responsibilities
  • Airflow coordinates when and under what conditions services interact
  • No service needs awareness of downstream consumers or execution order

This architecture reduces cross-service dependencies, improves service reusability and enables independent scaling and deployment.

docs.title: Built-in Reliability and Failure Semantics
docs.text:
Airflow provides failure handling as a core architectural feature:

  • Task-level retries with configurable backoff
  • Timeouts and execution limits
  • Partial re-runs without restarting from the beginning

This allows the system to recover gracefully from transient service outages, avoid cascading failures and maintain predictable operational behavior.

docs.title: Strong Observability and Operational Transparency
docs.text:
Airflow exposes execution state as part of its core model. DAGs and their tasks can be inspected visually, as well as logs and timestamps kept. Also, the historical audit trail of all workflow executions is kept.

These features provide immediate insight into system behavior and even controlled manual intervention when required.

docs.title: Technical Information
docs.text: Airflow's core components include the following, which form the backbone of its orchestration system:

docs.title: Scheduler
docs.text: The scheduler is the heart of Airflow. It continually monitors all DAGs and their tasks, triggering task instances once their dependencies are met. The scheduler is responsible for starting new DAG runs at the appropriate times (based on schedule or manual triggers) and determining which tasks are ready to run next. When a task is ready, the scheduler delegates its execution to an Executor, which will actually launch the task (possibly on a worker). The scheduler process runs indefinitely, polling the DAG definitions and the database for changes, and it orchestrates task execution in a continuous loop.

docs.title: Executor
docs.text:
The executor is the mechanism by which the scheduler distributes tasks for execution. It is configured as part of the scheduler (not a separate daemon). Different executors determine how and where tasks run. We have used the KubernetesExecutor, which launches each task in its own Kubernetes pod for isolation and scalability.

Regardless of executor type, the scheduler's job is to hand tasks to the executor, which then handles the low-level details of starting the task in the appropriate environment.

docs.title: Workers
docs.text: Workers are the processes (or containers) that actually execute the code of the tasks. In a simple setup using the LocalExecutor, the scheduler itself spawns worker processes internally to run tasks. In the distributed setup we have used, workers are separate processes (Kubernetes pods) that run on different machines. Workers continuously poll for tasks from the executor's queue and execute those tasks. Once finished, a worker will report the task's outcome back to the Airflow system (e.g. update task status in the database). Workers can be scaled out horizontally to run many tasks in parallel across multiple machines.

docs.title: Web Server
docs.text:
The web server is a FastAPI application that provides Airflow's user interface and RESTful APIs. It allows users to inspect DAGs, view task statuses, trigger runs, and debug workflows. The APIs provided are:

  • an internal API for workers to report status or fetch information while running tasks,
  • an internal API for the UI to dynamically fetch data (e.g. task updates) without direct database access,
  • and the public Airflow REST API for users to programmatically manage the Airflow instance.

The web server/API server does not execute DAG code; it simply displays information and handles user/worker requests. All sensitive operations (like running tasks) are handled by the scheduler and workers. The web server interacts with other components primarily through the metadata database or internal APIs. For security, in a distributed deployment the web server does not read DAG files directly - if a user views DAG code in the UI, it is fetched from the database (where the scheduler/DAG processor stored a serialized version of the DAG).

docs.title: Metadata Database
docs.text:
Airflow uses a persistent metadata database to store the state of the system. This database contains DAG definitions (serialized DAGs), task instance states (e.g. success, running, failed), DAG run records, scheduler metadata (like next run times), Airflow configurations, connections, variables, and history of past runs. Essentially, it is the single source of truth for the status of all workflows. Every component in Airflow interacts with this database:

  • The scheduler adds DAG run and task instance entries and updates their states as tasks progress.
  • Workers (or the tasks they run) update the database when tasks start, succeed, or fail (in newer versions this is done via the API server as an intermediary, rather than direct DB writes).
  • The web server reads from the database to display current DAG and task statuses in the UI.

Because of this central role, the metadata DB is a critical component; Airflow cannot run without it.

docs.title: DAG Files and DAG Processor
docs.text: Airflow DAGs are defined by Python files (DAG files) that users (DAG authors) write. These files need to be accessible to the Airflow system. The DAG processor is the component responsible for reading (parsing) these DAG files and storing their structure in the metadata DB for the scheduler to use. This means the DAG parsing is isolated from the main scheduler process, improving scheduler performance and security by clearly separating DAG code execution from scheduling logic. The DAG processor watches the DAG file directories (which can be local filesystems or object storage, depending on configuration), parses DAG definitions on change or at intervals, and saves a serialized version of each DAG to the database. This serialized DAG is what the scheduler actually uses to decide what tasks to run and when. In a multi-machine setup, DAG files must be distributed or synchronized to all places where they are needed (scheduler, any workers, and any triggerers) so that each component can access the latest DAG code. In our setup, this requirement is met by using NFS-mounted directories to ensure DAG files are consistently available across all Airflow components.

docs.title: Component Interaction and Communication
docs.text:
In a running Airflow deployment, these components work together to orchestrate workflows. Each component has a well-defined role, and they communicate mainly through the metadata database and, in some cases, through an inter-process messaging system (for task execution). The diagram below (from the official Airflow documentation) illustrates a typical Airflow architecture in a distributed setting with the core components separated:

Each arrow in the figure represents a communication or data flow between components.

docs.title: DAG Execution and Task Dependencies
docs.text:
Airflow manages workflow execution by enforcing the dependencies and order defined in each DAG. As mentioned above, a DAG is a directed acyclic graph where nodes are tasks and edges define dependencies (which task comes after which). These dependencies can be set in code (e.g. using task1 >> task2 or similar notation) and effectively create rules like "task2 cannot run until task1 has finished successfully". Here's how Airflow orchestrates tasks within a DAG, step by step:

  1. DAG Parsing and Scheduling: When a DAG (workflow) is added or updated, the DAG processor or scheduler will load that DAG file, parse the DAG's tasks and dependencies, and save a serialized DAG representation in the metadata database. The scheduler constantly evaluates DAGs to see if a new DAG run should be started - for example, if a DAG is scheduled to run every day at 9 AM, the scheduler will create a new DAG run at that time (if one isn't already running or queued). If a DAG is triggered manually (via UI or API), the scheduler also creates a DAG run promptly. Each DAG run is an instance of the workflow (often corresponding to a specific execution date or data interval).

  2. Dependency Checking and Task Queuing: Once a DAG run is initiated, the scheduler examines all tasks in that DAG to decide which tasks are ready to run. A task is ready when all its upstream dependencies in the DAG have succeeded (or are skipped, depending on trigger rules) or if it has no upstream dependencies at all. For the first tasks in the DAG (those with no predecessors, or whose predecessors are all done in previous runs), the scheduler will immediately mark them as runnable. The scheduler then puts these task instances into a queue via the executor. In this context, "queue" could be any message broker, or, in our case, the Kubernetes API server (K8s executor launching pods). The scheduler records in the database that those tasks are queued and in what state.

  3. Task Execution on Workers: Worker processes pick up the queued tasks and begin executing them. Each task instance runs the user-defined code. During execution, the task instance will log its output and may report heartbeat signals to the scheduler to indicate it's still running (this helps detect if tasks hang or the process died).

  4. Task Completion and Result Reporting: When a task finishes (successfully or with failure), it needs to report its state so that Airflow knows it's done. For security reasons, the task/worker does not directly touch the database. Instead, the worker makes a call to the API server, using an authenticated internal API. The API server in turn writes the delegated information to the metadata database on behalf of the worker. Similarly, if the task needs to fetch connection credentials or other info stored in Airflow's DB (e.g., to get a password from a connection), the worker will call an endpoint on the API server, which will retrieve the data from the DB and return it to the task at runtime. This mechanism enhances security by preventing direct database access from arbitrary task code while still providing the information and persistence needed.

  5. Scheduler Monitoring and Dependency Resolution: The scheduler is continually running in the background, polling the database for task updates. As soon as a task changes state (for example, from "running" to "success"), the scheduler takes note. It will then check if that task's completion satisfies any dependencies for downstream tasks. In each DAG run, tasks that were waiting on the now-completed task may become eligible to run. The scheduler thus transitions those tasks to the "queued" state and sends them to the executor, as described in step 2. This event-driven scheduling continues until all tasks in the DAG have been completed or the DAG run is otherwise finished (e.g., failed or stopped).

  6. Handling Task Dependencies and Triggers: By default, the Airflow scheduler applies the all-success trigger rule, meaning a task is eligible to run only after all of its upstream tasks have completed successfully. Airflow also supports more advanced dependency semantics that allow DAG authors to model complex workflows. Tasks can be configured to run when any upstream task succeeds or fails by adjusting their trigger rules. DAGs may also include branching logic, where the outcome of one task determines which downstream path is followed, with non-selected paths being skipped automatically. In addition, Airflow supports time-based and external dependencies through sensors. Deferrable sensors offload their waiting logic to the triggerer, allowing worker slots to remain free while external conditions are being met. Regardless of the complexity of the DAG structure, Airflow enforces dependency correctness by tracking task states in the metadata database and evaluating each DAG run as a whole. A task will never run before its declared prerequisites are satisfied. If an upstream failure is not tolerated by a downstream task's trigger rule, the downstream task will be skipped or marked as failed according to that rule.

  7. Parallelism and Concurrency: Airflow can run multiple tasks at the same time as long as they are ready to run and resources allow it. Tasks in the same DAG that have no dependencies on each other (or whose dependencies are already resolved) may be executed in parallel on different workers. Also, multiple DAGs can run concurrently. The system respects configured limits such as maximum concurrency per DAG and global worker pool limits (pools allow you to limit how many tasks of certain type or certain resource usage run simultaneously). The scheduler will not queue more tasks than the system can handle as per these limits. This ensures a single DAG cannot overwhelm the whole system if configured with appropriate limits. Airflow's design, using a central scheduler, ensures that even in highly parallel scenarios, the dependencies and order of execution are correctly maintained.

  8. User Monitoring and Intervention: Throughout a DAG run, the Airflow Web UI provides visibility into the state of the workflow. The UI (via the API server) fetches the latest task statuses and DAG run information from the metadata DB and displays the DAG's graph or grid view showing which tasks are queued, running, succeeded, or failed. Users can click on tasks to see logs (which the web server retrieves from the log storage), check XCom messages, or mark tasks for retry. If needed, users can intervene via the UI or CLI - for example, they can clear a task (reset its state to let it run again), trigger a backfill or a new run, or pause a DAG to stop scheduling new runs. These actions all update states in the database or send signals to the scheduler, which will then act on them (e.g., if you clear a failed task, the scheduler will treat it as pending and reschedule it). The architecture ensures that user actions are propagated to the scheduler through the same channels (DB or internal APIs), so the scheduler remains the single point orchestrating the actual execution.

Airflow's handling of task orchestration is designed to ensure that task dependencies are honored and that workflows run in the intended order despite a distributed execution. The combination of the scheduler's central brain, the state tracking in the metadata database, and workers executing tasks allows Airflow to reliably manage complex DAGs. It's worth noting that Airflow does not guarantee all tasks of a DAG run on the same worker or machine - tasks will run wherever there is capacity (which is why passing data between tasks is done through XCom or external storage, not local files). This distributed nature provides flexibility and scalability: as our workflow load grows, we can add more workers or another scheduler for redundancy, and Airflow will continue to orchestrate tasks in a consistent manner.

docs.title: Automations
docs.text: A number of automations are available to facilitate the development, quality assurance, security, deployment, maintenance and onboarding of the service. Here we describe some that are directly, publicly available.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
A GitHub Action workflow is available to generate documentation available in the project in the format presented here. The action is triggered manually and can be executed against the head of the repository. The documentation generated is versioned and the documentation version is expected as input to the workflow.

The documentation is built using the mkdocs library and specifically using the Material for mkdocs plugin. A number of additional tools are utilized, such as mike to support versioning, and others.

The documentation is generated and tagged with the provided version. It is uploaded to a dedicated documentation branch that is configured to be used as the base branch over which the repository GitHub Page presents its contents.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The orchestrator is configured in two layers:

  • Airflow configuration: the settings of the Airflow deployment itself, such as the executor, metadata database and logging. These follow the standard Airflow configuration reference.
  • Workflow configuration: the settings that the DataGEMS workflows need to reach the services they coordinate. These are provided as Airflow Variables and Connections.

docs.title: Workflow Configuration
docs.text: The workflow configuration covers the following areas.

docs.title: Integrated Services
docs.text:
Each DataGEMS service that the workflows call has its own configuration entry, which holds:

  • the service's base address,
  • the authorisation scope to request when calling it,
  • the paths of the operations the workflows use, and
  • for services with long-running jobs, how often the job status is checked.

The integrated services are the Platform Gateway, Data Model Management, MoMa management, the Profiler, the Streaming Interval Profiler, Cross-Dataset Discovery, Dataset Packaging, the Dataset Recommender and Dataset Linking.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: These are the address of the DataGEMS AAI and the orchestrator's client credentials. See Platform Integration.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: These are the locations of the staging area and of the dataset storage area that the Dataset Onboarding workflow uses. See Data Stores.

docs.title: Database Servers
docs.text: This is the list of database servers that host database-backed datasets, plus a default server. The Dataset Profiling workflow uses it to tell the Profiler how to reach a dataset stored in a relational database.

docs.title: Scheduled Workflows
docs.text: These are the settings for the scheduled workflows: the dataset monitored by Streaming Interval Profiling, and the observation source and time-series database connection used by Weather Observations Ingestion.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: Some configuration values are sensitive, such as client credentials and database connection details. Keep them separate from the rest of the configuration, using whatever the infrastructure offers: Kubernetes secrets, or an Airflow secrets backend. Never store them in the workflow code.

docs.title: Data Stores
docs.text: The orchestrator is mainly the data processing workflow layer that serves the related DataGEMS flows. Apart from the state of its workflow executions, it uses a small number of data stores to support specific workflows.

docs.title: Relational Database
docs.text:
The primary data store is a PostgreSQL relational database. It holds Airflow's metadata: workflow definitions, workflow runs, task states, execution history and related information.

The schema of this database is managed by Airflow.

docs.title: Dataset Storage
docs.text:
The Dataset Onboarding workflow uses shared storage that every orchestrator component can reach:

  • a staging area, where dataset files retrieved from external sources (files, HTTP or FTP) are placed, with one directory per dataset, and
  • a dataset storage area, where each dataset's data is kept for the rest of the platform. Data Model Management references this location for each dataset.

The orchestrator only places data in these areas. The services that consume it manage the datasets after that.

docs.title: Time-Series Database
docs.text: The Weather Observations Ingestion workflow stores weather station information and observations in a PostgreSQL database with time-series support (TimescaleDB). This store holds use-case data, not orchestrator state. Its connection is part of the workflow configuration.

docs.title: Updates
docs.text: When Airflow is updated to a newer version, any changes needed in the metadata database are applied by Airflow's migration process.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: The service is part of the DataGEMS platform offered through an existing deployment, following the DataGEMS release and deployment procedures over a managed infrastructure. The purpose of this section is not to detail the deployment processes put in place by the DataGEMS team.

docs.title: Helm Charts
docs.text: The service is offered as an existing Kubernetes Helm Chart.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: In order for the service to operate properly, the needed configuration values must be set to match the environment that it must operate in. The needed configuration is described in the relevant Configuration section.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: For the service to be able to operate, its underpinning services and dependencies must be available and accessible. The Architecture section describes the ecosystem in which the service needs to operate.

docs.title: Which workflows are available?
docs.text: The Workflow Overview lists every workflow, how it's started and what it does.

docs.title: How is a workflow started?
docs.text: Most workflows are started automatically by the DataGEMS platform as steps of a dataset's lifecycle. Authorised operators can also start them from the Airflow UI or through the Airflow REST API. Scheduled workflows run automatically at their configured interval. See Starting a Workflow.

docs.title: How can I follow the progress of a workflow?
docs.text: Workflows started by the platform report the status of each step back to the platform, so progress can be followed there. Operators can also look at each run, its tasks and their logs in the Airflow UI. See Platform Integration.

docs.title: Dataset onboarding failed at the staging step. What should I check?
docs.text: The staging step fails if any declared data location can't be retrieved. Check that every location is correct and reachable, for example that the URLs can be accessed and the FTP servers accept the connection. Also check that each location's kind matches the type of location. See Data Locations.

docs.title: Cross-Dataset Discovery indexing fails with "Dataset is not profiled". Why?
docs.text: Indexing needs the profile produced by the Dataset Profiling workflow. Run profiling successfully for the dataset first, then start indexing again.

docs.title: Can a failed workflow be resumed?
docs.text: Yes. Airflow keeps the state of every task, so an operator can clear a failed task in the Airflow UI and the run continues from that point, without repeating the tasks that already succeeded.

docs.title: Known Issues
docs.text: Known issues and their status are tracked in the GitHub issues of the repository.

docs.title: Platform Integration
docs.text:
The Data Workflow Orchestrator doesn't work in isolation. It's the coordination layer between the DataGEMS platform, which decides what should happen to a dataset, and the DataGEMS services that do the work. This page describes how the orchestrator fits into the platform.

flowchart LR
    P[DataGEMS Platform] -- starts workflow --> O[Data Workflow Orchestrator]
    O -- reports progress & completion --> P
    O -- authenticated requests --> S[DataGEMS Services<br/>Data Model Management, Profiler,<br/>Cross-Dataset Discovery, Packaging,<br/>Recommender, Dataset Linking]
    O -- obtains access tokens --> A[DataGEMS AAI]

docs.title: Platform Processes
docs.text:
The DataGEMS platform manages each dataset's lifecycle as a process made of steps, such as onboarding, profiling and indexing. When a step needs a workflow, the platform starts the matching workflow in the orchestrator. The run parameters include:

  • the dataset's identifier and any information the workflow needs, and
  • workflow_process_step_information, which identifies the process and step that the run belongs to.

Users don't need to provide workflow_process_step_information themselves. The platform supplies it, and the orchestrator uses it to report back to the right step.

docs.title: Progress Reporting
docs.text:
While a platform-started workflow runs, each task reports its lifecycle events to the platform:

Event Reported step status Task started In progress Task retrying In progress Task succeeded In progress (or succeeded, for the workflow's final task) Task skipped In progress Task failed Failed

Each report includes a summary of the task's execution, which lets the platform show detailed progress and help diagnose failures.

When the final task of a workflow succeeds, its success callback sends a completion notification for that kind of step (for example, onboarding complete or profiling complete). This notification is what moves the dataset forward: on receiving it, the platform starts the next workflow of the dataset's lifecycle. The workflows of a lifecycle therefore run one at a time, in a predetermined order, and never in parallel. If a workflow fails, no completion notification is sent and the next workflow isn't started. See Workflow Overview for the order.

Scheduled workflows such as Streaming Interval Profiling and Weather Observations Ingestion aren't part of a platform process, so they don't send these reports.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
All requests from the orchestrator to other DataGEMS services are authenticated through the DataGEMS Authentication and Authorisation Infrastructure (AAI):

  • The orchestrator authenticates as a service, with its own client credentials (OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant).
  • It requests a separate access token for each target service, limited to that service's scope. Each workflow therefore gets only the access it needs.
  • Tokens are reused while they're valid and renewed automatically before they expire.

The credentials are part of the deployment's protected configuration. See Configuration.

docs.title: Maintenance
docs.text: The service is part of the DataGEMS platform offered through an existing deployment, following the DataGEMS release and deployment procedures over a managed infrastructure along with the maintenance activities that are scheduled within the platform. The purpose of this section is not to detail the maintenance activities put in place by the DataGEMS team.

docs.title: Healthchecks
docs.text:
The service observability documentation describes healthcheck endpoints that can be used to track the status of the service.

An example of a healthcheck response that returns 200 OK for healthy state is: 

{
  "metadatabase":{
    "status":"healthy"
  },
  "scheduler":{
    "status":"healthy",
    "latest_scheduler_heartbeat":"2018-12-26 17:15:11+00:00"
  },
  "triggerer":{
    "status":"healthy",
    "latest_triggerer_heartbeat":"2018-12-26 17:16:12+00:00"
  },
  "dag_processor":{
    "status":"healthy",
    "latest_dag_processor_heartbeat":"2018-12-26 17:16:12+00:00"
  }
}

docs.title: Versions & Updates
docs.text: The service follows the versioning and update scheme that Airflow supports.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
All state persisted by the service is maintained in the relational database as described in the respective datastores section.

To keep backups of the state, the respective utilities must be scheduled to run in a consistent manner.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Troubleshooting is primarily done through the logging mechanisms that are available within Airflow. These offer log reports on individual tasks and flows as they are executed by the Airflow engine.

docs.title: Onboarding Material
docs.text: This section contains some references and material that will assist users and integrators onboarding process.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
The definite guide for integrators remains the Airflow documentation and API reference.

Airflow is an open source project and the codebase is available under Apache License Version 2.0 in the project's GitHub code repository.

Custom workflows applying for the DataGEMS use cases are available under Apache License Version 2.0 in our GitHub code repository.

More information on the workflows supported for the DataGEMS data management needs can be found at the Workflow Overview section.

For an overall view of the service, you can go through the Architecture.

For any questions, you can consult the FAQ.

If you are facing a problem, check if there is a relevant issue answering your question.

You can always contact us through the DataGEMS Help Desk.

docs.title: Quality Assurance
docs.text:
Key aspects of the Quality Assurance checklist that DataGEMS services must pass have been defined in the processes and documents governing the platform development and quality assurance.

docs.title: Cross-Dataset Discovery Indexing Workflow
docs.text:
The Cross-Dataset Discovery Indexing Workflow (CDD_INGEST) adds a dataset to the index of the Cross-Dataset Discovery service, so that it can be found through discovery queries that span the platform's datasets.

The dataset must have been profiled before it can be indexed. See Dataset Profiling. In a dataset's lifecycle, this is the last workflow of the chain: the platform starts it after Recommender Registration completes. See Workflow Overview.

docs.title: Input
docs.text: Parameter Type Format Mandatory Description id string uuid yes Identifier of the dataset to index. workflow_process_step_information object yes Tracking information for the platform process step that this run belongs to. Supplied automatically by the platform. See Platform Integration.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Fetch Ingestion File] --> B[Begin Ingestion]
    B --> C{Is indexing complete?}
    C -- No, check again later --> C
    C -- Yes --> D((End))

docs.title: Fetch Ingestion File
docs.text: This task asks the Profiler service for the location of the dataset's discovery profile, which was produced during profiling. If the dataset has no discovery profile yet, the workflow stops with a failure that says the dataset hasn't been profiled.

docs.title: Begin Ingestion
docs.text: This task submits an indexing job for the discovery profile to the Cross-Dataset Discovery service, and returns the identifier of the job.

docs.title: Wait for Completion
docs.text: This task checks the indexing job's status at regular intervals until the job completes, releasing its worker slot between checks. If the job fails, the workflow stops with a failure.

docs.title: Completion
docs.text: When indexing completes, the workflow notifies the platform that the dataset is available for cross-dataset discovery. This completes the dataset's lifecycle chain.

docs.title: Dataset Linking Report Workflow
docs.text: The Dataset Linking Report Workflow (DATASET_LINKING_REPORT) asks the Dataset Linking service to produce a report on how similar datasets are, and how they could be linked, based on their keywords, descriptions and headlines.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
All tuning parameters are optional. If a parameter isn't set, the Dataset Linking service uses its own default.

Parameter Type Mandatory Description id string (uuid) yes Identifier of the dataset that the report is requested for. kw number no Weight of keyword similarity in the overall similarity score. desc number no Weight of description similarity in the overall similarity score. head number no Weight of headline similarity in the overall similarity score. th number (0–100) no Similarity threshold, as a percentage, that a pair of datasets must reach to be reported as related. keyword_method jaccard or sbert no Method used to compare keywords: set overlap (Jaccard) or semantic embeddings (SBERT). Defaults to jaccard. include_chunks boolean no Whether to include the matching parts of descriptions as evidence in the report. include_graphs boolean no Whether to generate graphs while the report is built. graphs_only_above_threshold boolean no Whether to generate graphs only for pairs that reach the threshold. workflow_process_step_information object yes Tracking information for the platform process step that this run belongs to. Supplied automatically by the platform. See Platform Integration.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Start Report Job] --> B{Is the report complete?}
    B -- No, check again later --> B
    B -- Yes --> C((End))

docs.title: Start Report Job
docs.text: This task submits a report job to the Dataset Linking service with the provided parameters, and returns the identifier of the job.

docs.title: Wait for Completion
docs.text: This task checks the report job's status at regular intervals until the job completes, releasing its worker slot between checks. If the job fails, the workflow stops with a failure.

docs.title: Completion
docs.text: When the report is complete, the workflow notifies the platform, which can then retrieve the report from the Dataset Linking service. The platform then starts the next step of the dataset's lifecycle, the Dataset Packaging workflow.

docs.title: Dataset Onboarding Workflow
docs.text: The Dataset Onboarding Workflow (DATASET_ONBOARDING) provides a unified, controlled process for bringing a dataset into the platform, wherever it is originally stored. It accepts the dataset's metadata together with one or more data locations, makes the data available in the platform's storage, and registers the dataset in the Data Model Management service.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
The workflow accepts the following parameters:

Parameter Type Format Mandatory Description id string uuid yes Globally unique identifier of the dataset. It's used throughout the workflow to associate metadata, stored files and lifecycle events with the same dataset. dataLocations string JSON array yes JSON-encoded list of the locations where the dataset's data can be found. See Data Locations. name string no Human-readable name of the dataset. description string no Detailed description of the dataset's contents, scope and purpose. headline string no Short, high-level summary of the dataset, typically shown in listings. fields_of_science array of strings no Scientific or domain classifications of the dataset. languages array of strings no Languages represented in the dataset's content. keywords array of strings no Free-form keywords that improve discoverability. countries array of strings no Countries relevant to the dataset, such as its geographic coverage. publishedUrl string uri no Public URL where the dataset is published or described. citeAs string no Recommended citation for the dataset. license string no License under which the dataset is distributed. doi string no Digital Object Identifier of the dataset, if one exists. date_published string date no Publication date of the dataset. Defaults to the current date. userId string no Identifier of the user who requested the onboarding, used for attribution and provenance. workflow_process_step_information object yes Tracking information for the platform process step that this run belongs to. Supplied automatically by the platform. See Platform Integration.

docs.title: Data Locations
docs.text:
Each entry in dataLocations is an object with a kind and a location:

[
  { "kind": "Http", "location": "https://example.org/data/measurements.csv" },
  { "kind": "Ftp",  "location": "ftp://ftp.example.org/pub/measurements.csv" }
]

kind can be given by name or by its numeric value:

Kind Value Description File 0 The data is a file on a filesystem that's accessible to the orchestrator. Http 1 The data can be downloaded from an HTTP(S) URL. Ftp 2 The data can be downloaded from an FTP server. The location is an FTP URI. Remote 3 The data is in a remote store that the platform accesses directly. Staged 4 The data is already in the platform's storage. Database 5 The data is in a relational database. The location identifies the database.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Stage Dataset Files] --> B[Register Dataset]
    B --> C[Load Dataset]
    C --> D((Finish))

docs.title: Stage Dataset Files
docs.text:
This task makes sure the dataset's data is available in the platform's storage area before the dataset is registered. Datasets come from many kinds of storage, so this step normalises them: downstream steps always work with locations that the platform controls.

All declared locations are processed in parallel:

  • File, Http and Ftp locations are retrieved and stored in a staging area dedicated to the dataset. Each stored file gets a unique name, so files never collide.
  • Remote, Staged and Database locations are already accessible to the platform and are passed on unchanged.

The task outputs the effective list of locations for the dataset. If any location can't be accessed or stored, the workflow fails at this step, so a dataset is never partially onboarded.

docs.title: Register Dataset
docs.text:
This task registers the dataset and its metadata in the Data Model Management service, which makes the dataset discoverable, traceable and addressable in the platform. The registration also records provenance: which user requested the onboarding and when.

If registration fails, the workflow stops. A dataset is never loaded unless it has been registered.

docs.title: Load Dataset
docs.text:
This task completes onboarding by informing the Data Model Management service that the dataset's data is in its final storage location, and updating the dataset's state. It doesn't change the metadata recorded at registration.

If the storage location isn't available yet when this step runs (for example, because an upstream process is still making it available), the step automatically retries a few times. Any other error fails the workflow immediately. The dataset stays registered, so the problem can be investigated and loading retried.

docs.title: Completion
docs.text: When the dataset has been loaded, the workflow notifies the platform that onboarding has finished. The notification includes how the dataset is stored (file-based or in a relational database), so the platform can configure and start the Dataset Profiling workflow, which is the next step of the dataset's lifecycle.

docs.title: Dataset Packaging Workflow
docs.text: The Dataset Packaging Workflow (DATASET_PACKAGING) asks the Dataset Packaging service to package a dataset that's already on the platform, so it can be distributed and reused.

docs.title: Input
docs.text: Parameter Type Format Mandatory Description id string uuid yes Identifier of the dataset to package. workflow_process_step_information object yes Tracking information for the platform process step that this run belongs to. Supplied automatically by the platform. See Platform Integration.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Import Dataset] --> B((End))

docs.title: Import Dataset
docs.text: This task submits the dataset to the Dataset Packaging service. The service retrieves the dataset's information from the platform and handles the packaging itself. If the request is rejected, the workflow stops with a failure.

docs.title: Completion
docs.text: When the request is accepted, the workflow notifies the platform that the packaging step is complete. The platform then starts the next step of the dataset's lifecycle, the Recommender Registration workflow.

docs.title: Dataset Profiling Workflow
docs.text: The Dataset Profiling Workflow (DATASET_PROFILING) runs the whole profiling process for an onboarded dataset. It asks the Profiler service to generate a profile, adds the result to the dataset's representation in Data Model Management, and then releases the profiling resources.

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
The workflow accepts the following parameters:

Parameter Type Format Mandatory Description id string uuid yes Globally unique identifier of the dataset to profile. Profiling results are linked to the dataset through this identifier. data_store_kind integer 0 or 1 yes How the dataset is stored: 0 for file-based storage, 1 for a relational database. Determines how the Profiler accesses the data. Defaults to 0. database_name string when data_store_kind is 1 Name of the database that holds the dataset. name string no Human-readable name of the dataset. description string no Detailed description of the dataset. headline string no Short, high-level summary of the dataset. keywords array of strings no Free-form keywords associated with the dataset. fields_of_science array of strings no Scientific or domain classifications of the dataset. languages array of strings no Languages represented in the dataset's content. Relevant when profiling textual data. countries array of strings no Countries relevant to the dataset. url string uri no Public URL where the dataset is published or described. citeAs string no Recommended citation for the dataset. conformsTo string no Standard, schema or specification that the dataset conforms to. license string no License under which the dataset is distributed. doi string no Digital Object Identifier of the dataset, if one exists. date_published string date no Publication date of the dataset. Defaults to the current date. archivedAt string no Location where the dataset is archived. dataset_file_path string no Path to the dataset's files, when known. userId string no Identifier of the user who requested profiling, used for attribution. workflow_process_step_information object yes Tracking information for the platform process step that this run belongs to. Supplied automatically by the platform. See Platform Integration.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Trigger Profile] --> B{Is the profile ready?}
    B -- No, check again later --> B
    B -- Yes --> C[Fetch Profile]
    C --> D[Convert Profile]
    D --> E[Update Data Model Management]
    E --> F[Profile Cleanup]
    F --> G((End))

docs.title: Trigger Profile
docs.text:
This task submits a profiling job to the Profiler service. The request includes the dataset's descriptive metadata and a data connector that tells the Profiler how to reach the data:

  • For file-based datasets, the Profiler finds the data from the dataset identifier.
  • For database-backed datasets, the orchestrator finds the database server that hosts the named database in its configured list of database servers, and passes the connection details to the Profiler.

The task returns the identifier of the profiling job.

docs.title: Wait for Completion
docs.text: This task checks the profiling job's status at regular intervals until the profile is ready. Between checks it releases its worker slot, so long-running profiling jobs don't use execution resources. If the job fails, or is no longer available, the workflow stops with a failure, so incomplete or invalid profiles never reach downstream systems.

docs.title: Fetch Profile
docs.text: When the profile is ready, this task retrieves it from the Profiler service unchanged, in its original structured (Croissant-based) form.

docs.title: Convert Profile
docs.text: This task converts the profile into the property-graph (PG-JSON) representation used by the DataGEMS metadata model (MoMa), using the MoMa management service.

docs.title: Update Data Model Management
docs.text: This task updates the dataset in the Data Model Management service. It combines the converted profile with the descriptive information from the original profile in a single update, along with provenance for the profiling operation. When this step succeeds, the dataset's profile is available on the platform.

docs.title: Profile Cleanup
docs.text: After the profile has been safely stored, this task asks the Profiler service to release the resources of the profiling job. Cleanup runs only after the results are stored, so no information is lost.

docs.title: Completion
docs.text: When cleanup finishes, the workflow notifies the platform that profiling is complete. The platform then starts the next step of the dataset's lifecycle, the Dataset Linking Report workflow.

docs.title: Recommender Registration Workflow
docs.text: The Recommender Registration Workflow (DATASET_RECOMMENDATION_REGISTERING) registers a dataset with the Dataset Recommender service, so that the dataset can be recommended to platform users.

docs.title: Input
docs.text: Parameter Type Format Mandatory Description id string uuid yes Identifier of the dataset to register. workflow_process_step_information object yes Tracking information for the platform process step that this run belongs to. Supplied automatically by the platform. See Platform Integration.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Import Dataset] --> B((End))

docs.title: Import Dataset
docs.text: This task submits the dataset to the Dataset Recommender service, which retrieves the dataset's information from the platform and adds the dataset to its recommendation catalogue. If the request is rejected, the workflow stops with a failure.

docs.title: Completion
docs.text: When registration succeeds, the workflow notifies the platform that the recommender registration step is complete. The platform then starts the next step of the dataset's lifecycle, the Cross-Dataset Discovery Indexing workflow.

docs.title: Workflow Overview
docs.text: The Data Workflow Orchestrator hosts the data management workflows of the DataGEMS platform. Each workflow is an Airflow DAG that coordinates one or more DataGEMS services to complete a step of a dataset's lifecycle, from making the data available to profiling, indexing and packaging it.

docs.title: Available Workflows
docs.text:
Workflow DAG ID Started by Purpose Dataset Onboarding DATASET_ONBOARDING Platform Brings a dataset's files into the platform's storage and registers the dataset and its metadata in Data Model Management. Dataset Profiling DATASET_PROFILING Platform Generates a profile of an onboarded dataset and enriches its representation in Data Model Management. Dataset Linking Report DATASET_LINKING_REPORT Platform Produces a report of similarities and links between datasets. Dataset Packaging DATASET_PACKAGING Platform Asks the Dataset Packaging service to package a dataset. Recommender Registration DATASET_RECOMMENDATION_REGISTERING Platform Registers a dataset with the Dataset Recommender service. Cross-Dataset Discovery Indexing CDD_INGEST Platform Indexes a profiled dataset in the Cross-Dataset Discovery service so it can be found through discovery queries. Streaming Interval Profiling STREAMING_INTERVAL_PROFILING Schedule Keeps the metadata of a continuously updated dataset in sync with its latest data interval. Weather Observations Ingestion GEO_INGEST Schedule Collects weather station observations for use-case datasets.

The typical lifecycle of a newly contributed dataset chains several of these workflows in a fixed order:

flowchart LR
    A[Dataset Onboarding] --> B[Dataset Profiling]
    B --> C[Dataset Linking Report]
    C --> D[Dataset Packaging]
    D --> E[Recommender Registration]
    E --> F[Cross-Dataset Discovery Indexing]

The workflows run one at a time, never in parallel. The platform starts each workflow in this predetermined order, and the chain is driven by completion callbacks:

  1. The platform starts the first workflow of the chain.
  2. When the final task of a workflow succeeds, its success callback notifies the platform that the step is complete.
  3. The platform then starts the next workflow in the chain.

A workflow is therefore only started after the previous one has completed successfully. If a workflow fails, the platform isn't notified of completion and the next workflow isn't started. Each workflow only performs its own step. See Platform Integration.

docs.title: Common Behaviour
docs.text:
All workflows share the following characteristics:

  • Parameterised runs: each run receives its inputs as run parameters. The parameters of each workflow are listed on its page.
  • Authenticated service calls: every call to another DataGEMS service is authenticated on behalf of the orchestrator. See Platform Integration.
  • Status reporting: workflows started by the platform report the progress of each task back to it, so the dataset's status can be followed from the platform. See Platform Integration.
  • Efficient waiting: when a workflow waits for a long-running job in another service (for example a profiling or indexing job), it checks the job's status at regular intervals. Between checks it releases its worker slot, so waiting doesn't consume execution resources.
  • Fail-fast execution: if a step can't be completed, the workflow stops and is marked as failed instead of continuing with incomplete results.

docs.title: Starting a Workflow
docs.text:
Platform workflows are normally started by the DataGEMS platform as part of its dataset management processes. Authorised operators can also start them from the Airflow UI or through the Airflow REST API, passing the workflow parameters as the run configuration (conf).

Scheduled workflows run automatically at their configured interval and take no parameters.

docs.title: Streaming Interval Profiling Workflow
docs.text: The Streaming Interval Profiling Workflow (STREAMING_INTERVAL_PROFILING) keeps the metadata of a continuously updated (streaming) dataset in line with its most recent data. It runs on a schedule. At each run it gets a profile of the latest data interval and applies the changes to the dataset's representation in Data Model Management.

docs.title: Schedule and Input
docs.text: The workflow runs automatically every hour and takes no run parameters. The dataset it monitors is set in the orchestrator's configuration.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Fetch Interval Profile] --> B[Update Dataset Metadata]
    B --> C((End))

docs.title: Fetch Interval Profile
docs.text: This task asks the Streaming Interval Profiler service to profile the latest interval of the monitored dataset. The response describes the changes to apply to the dataset's metadata: updated properties of existing metadata elements, and new elements to add.

docs.title: Update Dataset Metadata
docs.text:
This task retrieves the dataset's current representation from the Data Model Management service and applies the reported changes:

  • properties of existing elements are replaced with their updated values,
  • new elements and the relationships between them are added.

The updated representation is then sent back to Data Model Management.

docs.title: Status Reporting
docs.text: This workflow runs on a schedule, not as part of a platform process, so it doesn't report step status to the platform. Its runs can be followed in the Airflow UI.

docs.title: Weather Observations Ingestion Workflow
docs.text: The Weather Observations Ingestion Workflow (GEO_INGEST) collects observations from a network of meteorological stations and stores them in a time-series database. Over time it builds a continuously growing dataset for DataGEMS use cases that rely on weather data.

docs.title: Schedule and Input
docs.text: The workflow runs automatically every 10 minutes and takes no run parameters. The observation source and the target database are set in the orchestrator's configuration.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Fetch Weather] --> B[Store Data]
    B --> C((End))

docs.title: Fetch Weather
docs.text: This task retrieves the latest station observations from the meteorological data provider, as a GeoJSON feature collection. Each feature describes one station (its identifier, name and coordinates) and its latest measurements, such as temperature, humidity, pressure, rainfall and wind.

docs.title: Store Data
docs.text:
This task stores the retrieved data in the time-series database:

  • Stations are created or updated, so station information stays current.
  • Observations are appended. Observations that are already stored are ignored, so overlapping collections never create duplicates.

The outcome of each collection is also recorded, so the completeness of the collected data can be monitored.

See Data Stores for more on the time-series database.

docs.title: Status Reporting
docs.text: This workflow runs on a schedule, not as part of a platform process, so it doesn't report step status to the platform. Its runs can be followed in the Airflow UI.
